track_subtitle: Focused one-task SQL practice using original Career Accelerator datasets and the native DuckDB editor.

authoring_policy.task_limit: Exactly one required task per exercise. A second task is allowed only when inseparable from the same result.
authoring_policy.originality: All learner-facing wording, scenarios, schemas, records, solutions, hints, and expected outputs are original Career Accelerator content.
authoring_policy.source_use: External challenges are credited only as structure and concept blueprints.
authoring_policy.scope: Every exercise tests one primary concept and uses only SQL taught by its terminal DataCamp chapter.

exercises.title: Create Customer Display Names

source.challenge: Combine first and last names into one full-name column
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Build one readable display field from two source columns and name it clearly.
exercises.scenario: Northstar support agents need one clean customer label for a new case-assignment screen.
exercises.task: Return each customer ID with the customer’s first and last name combined as `customer_name`.
result_requirements: Sort by `customer_id` from lowest to highest.
hints: Use the text-concatenation operator between the two name columns.
Add a single space between the first and last name.
Give the completed expression the alias `customer_name`, then sort by the ID.

exercises.title: Filter Urgent Open Cases

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Use more than one condition to keep only the records a manager requested.
exercises.scenario: The support director is preparing a same-day escalation list.
exercises.task: Return the open support cases whose priority is `Critical`.
result_requirements: Sort by `case_id` from lowest to highest.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT case_id, subject, assigned_team
      FROM support_cases
      WHERE status = 'Open' AND priority = 'Critical'
      ORDER BY case_id;
hints: Start by filtering the `status` column.
Add a second condition for the requested priority.
Both conditions must be true for a row to remain.

exercises.title: Count Resolved Cases by Team

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Count matching records at the requested business grain.
exercises.scenario: The operations lead wants a quick view of which teams closed the most cases.
exercises.task: Count resolved cases for each assigned team.
result_requirements: Show only teams with at least one resolved case.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT assigned_team, COUNT(*) AS resolved_case_count
      FROM support_cases
      WHERE status = 'Resolved'
      GROUP BY assigned_team
      ORDER BY resolved_case_count DESC, assigned_team;
hints: Filter to resolved cases before grouping.
Each output row should represent one assigned team.
Count the rows in each team and sort the largest count first.

exercises.title: Find Southeast Customers Missing Phone Numbers

source.challenge: Combine filters and require a recorded value
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Combine a text filter with a missing-value condition and deterministic sorting.
exercises.scenario: The customer-success team is cleaning contact details before an outreach campaign.
exercises.task: Return Southeast customers who do not have a phone number recorded.
result_requirements: Sort by `city`, then `last_name`, then `customer_id`, all ascending.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, city
      FROM customers
      WHERE region_code = 'SE' AND phone IS NULL
      ORDER BY city, last_name, customer_id;
hints: Use `IS NULL` rather than comparing the phone column with an empty string.
The region and missing-phone conditions must both be true.
Use three sort fields so the result is stable.

exercises.title: Show Customers with Full Region Names

source.challenge: Join patients to full province names
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Connect two tables through a matching key and select fields from both.
exercises.scenario: The reporting team wants readable region names instead of internal region codes.
exercises.task: Return every customer with the full name of the customer’s region.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
             c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name,
             r.region_name
      FROM customers AS c
      INNER JOIN regions AS r ON c.region_code = r.region_code
      ORDER BY c.customer_id;
hints: The shared key is `region_code`.
Use one table alias for customers and another for regions.
Build the display name from the customer table after the join.

exercises.title: List Employees Assigned to Sponsored Projects

source.challenge: Produce a list of all members who have used a tennis court
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Join three related tables to produce one deduplicated assignment list.
exercises.scenario: Program leadership needs to know who is working on each sponsored initiative.
exercises.task: List every project assignment with the project name, employee name, and allocated hours.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT p.project_name, e.employee_name, a.hours_allocated
      FROM project_assignments AS a
      INNER JOIN projects AS p ON a.project_id = p.project_id
      INNER JOIN employees AS e ON a.employee_id = e.employee_id
      ORDER BY p.project_name, e.employee_name;
hints: Start from the assignment table because it contains both keys.
Join projects using `project_id`.
Join employees using `employee_id`, then select the readable names.

exercises.title: Show Employees and Their Managers

source.challenge: Produce a list of all members, along with their recommender
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Preserve every employee while looking up an optional manager in the same table.
exercises.scenario: HR needs an organization-directory extract that still includes department heads without managers.
exercises.task: Return every employee with the employee’s manager name when one exists.
result_requirements: Use `NULL` for employees without a manager.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT e.employee_name, m.employee_name AS manager_name
      FROM employees AS e
      LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id
      ORDER BY e.employee_name;
hints: Use the employees table twice with different aliases.
The employee row should be on the preserved side of the join.
Match the employee’s `manager_id` to the manager alias’s `employee_id`.

exercises.title: Combine Members and Guests into One Booking List

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Combine compatible result sets into one duplicate-free list.
exercises.scenario: The facilities coordinator needs one list from the `bookings` table showing whether each booking belongs to a member or a guest. The `booking_type` field does not exist in the dataset; create it as a text alias in each SELECT.
exercises.task: Using the `bookings` table, return each `booking_id` and create a calculated text column named `booking_type`. Label rows with a nonzero `member_id` as `Member`, label rows with `member_id = 0` as `Guest`, and combine the two compatible queries with `UNION`.
result_requirements: Use the `bookings` table for both SELECT statements.
Return `booking_id` and a calculated alias named `booking_type`.
Use `'Member' AS booking_type` when `member_id <> 0` and `'Guest' AS booking_type` when `member_id = 0`.
Combine the two result sets with `UNION` and sort by `booking_id`.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT booking_id, 'Member' AS booking_type
      FROM bookings
      WHERE member_id <> 0
      UNION
      SELECT booking_id, 'Guest' AS booking_type
      FROM bookings
      WHERE member_id = 0
      ORDER BY booking_id;
hints: `booking_type` is not a stored column. Create it by selecting a text literal with `AS booking_type`.
Write one query against `bookings` for nonzero member IDs and a second query against `bookings` for member ID 0.
Both queries must return `booking_id` followed by the calculated `booking_type`, then be combined with `UNION`.

exercises.title: Count Employees and Assignments by Department

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Aggregate a small relational hierarchy without multiplying counts.
exercises.scenario: Leadership wants a department-level staffing summary that distinguishes employees from project assignments.
exercises.task: For each department, count distinct employees and distinct project assignments.
result_requirements: Include departments with no project assignments.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT d.department_name,
             COUNT(DISTINCT e.employee_id) AS employee_count,
             COUNT(DISTINCT (a.project_id, a.employee_id)) AS assignment_count
      FROM departments AS d
      LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON d.department_id = e.department_id
      LEFT JOIN project_assignments AS a ON e.employee_id = a.employee_id
      GROUP BY d.department_name
      ORDER BY d.department_name;
hints: Preserve departments by starting from the department table.
Joining assignments can repeat employee rows, so count employee IDs distinctly.
An assignment is identified by the project-and-employee pair.

exercises.title: Find Bookings Above Their Facility Average

source.challenge: Produce a list of costly bookings, using a subquery
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Compare each row with an aggregate calculated for its own group.
exercises.scenario: The facilities manager wants unusually long bookings reviewed by facility.
exercises.task: Return bookings whose slot count is greater than the average slot count for the same facility.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT b.booking_id, b.facility_id, b.slots
      FROM bookings AS b
      WHERE b.slots > (
          SELECT AVG(b2.slots)
          FROM bookings AS b2
          WHERE b2.facility_id = b.facility_id
      )
      ORDER BY b.facility_id, b.booking_id;
hints: The comparison value is different for each facility.
The inner query should average slots only for the current outer facility.
Correlate the inner facility ID with the outer booking alias.

exercises.title: Classify Orders by Value

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Turn numeric values into clear business categories.
exercises.scenario: The sales team wants a simple size label for completed orders.
exercises.task: Classify each completed order as `Small`, `Standard`, or `Large` based on its total amount.
result_requirements: Use `Small` below 100, `Standard` from 100 through 299.99, and `Large` at 300 or more.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT order_id, total_amount,
             CASE
               WHEN total_amount < 100 THEN 'Small'
               WHEN total_amount < 300 THEN 'Standard'
               ELSE 'Large'
             END AS order_size
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'Completed'
      ORDER BY order_id;
hints: Evaluate the smallest range first.
The second condition only needs to test the upper limit because smaller values have already been handled.
Use `ELSE` for orders of 300 or more.

exercises.title: Find Orders Above the Overall Average

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Use a one-value subquery as a filter threshold.
exercises.scenario: Finance wants to review completed orders that are larger than the typical completed order.
exercises.task: Return completed orders whose total amount is greater than the average completed-order amount.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'Completed'
        AND total_amount > (
          SELECT AVG(total_amount)
          FROM orders
          WHERE status = 'Completed'
        )
      ORDER BY total_amount DESC, order_id;
hints: The inner query should return exactly one number.
Use the same completed-order filter inside and outside the subquery.
Compare each outer order total with the average returned by the inner query.

exercises.title: Identify High-Value Repeat Customers

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Build a readable multi-stage query that calculates customer metrics before filtering.
exercises.scenario: Customer success wants a list of repeat buyers whose completed-order value is at least 400 dollars.
exercises.task: Return customers with at least two completed orders and at least 400 dollars in completed-order value.
exercises.solution_sql:
WITH customer_metrics AS (
        SELECT customer_id,
               COUNT(*) AS completed_orders,
               SUM(total_amount) AS completed_value
        FROM orders
        WHERE status = 'Completed'
        GROUP BY customer_id
      )
      SELECT c.customer_id,
             c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name,
             m.completed_orders,
             ROUND(m.completed_value, 2) AS completed_value
      FROM customer_metrics AS m
      INNER JOIN customers AS c ON m.customer_id = c.customer_id
      WHERE m.completed_orders >= 2 AND m.completed_value >= 400
      ORDER BY completed_value DESC, c.customer_id;
hints: Create one CTE at the customer grain.
Calculate both the order count and total value inside the CTE.
Join the summarized rows to customers only after the metrics are calculated.

exercises.title: Add the Total Customer Count to Every Row

source.challenge: Produce member names with the total member count on every row
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Add overall context without collapsing row-level results.
exercises.scenario: A customer export needs the total number of customers repeated beside every customer row.
exercises.task: Return each customer with the total customer count shown on every row.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT customer_id,
             first_name || ' ' || last_name AS customer_name,
             COUNT(*) OVER () AS total_customers
      FROM customers
      ORDER BY customer_id;
hints: A normal `COUNT` with `GROUP BY` would collapse rows.
Use `COUNT(*)` as a window function.
An empty window specification means the count uses the full result set.

exercises.title: Number Sessions Within Each Team

source.challenge: Produce a numbered list of members
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Number rows independently inside each group.

gate.course: PostgreSQL Summary Stats and Window Functions

exercises.scenario: Team leads want each work session numbered from earliest to latest within the team.
exercises.task: Assign a sequence number to every work session within its team.
result_requirements: Number rows by `session_date`, then `session_id` within each team.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT team, session_date, employee_id,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY team
               ORDER BY session_date, session_id
             ) AS team_session_number
      FROM work_sessions
      ORDER BY team, team_session_number;
hints: The numbering restarts for each team.
Use the team column in `PARTITION BY`.
Put the chronological fields inside the window’s `ORDER BY`.

exercises.title: Rank Employees by Logged Hours

source.challenge: Rank members by rounded hours used
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Rank aggregated results while preserving ties.

gate.course: PostgreSQL Summary Stats and Window Functions

exercises.scenario: Operations wants an hours leaderboard that gives tied employees the same rank.
exercises.task: Rank employees by their total logged hours from highest to lowest.
exercises.solution_sql:
WITH employee_hours AS (
        SELECT employee_id, ROUND(SUM(hours), 1) AS total_hours
        FROM work_sessions
        GROUP BY employee_id
      )
      SELECT employee_id, total_hours,
             RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_hours DESC) AS hours_rank
      FROM employee_hours
      ORDER BY hours_rank, employee_id;
hints: Aggregate to one row per employee before ranking.
Rank the total in descending order.
Use `RANK`, not `ROW_NUMBER`, so equal totals share a rank.

exercises.title: Group Consecutive Task Dates into Projects

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Use neighboring rows to identify the beginning of each consecutive date sequence.

gate.course: PostgreSQL Summary Stats and Window Functions

exercises.scenario: A delivery log stores one-day task intervals, but leadership wants the larger continuous project periods.
exercises.task: Combine consecutive task intervals into project start and end dates.
result_requirements: Sort shorter projects first; break ties by `project_start`.
exercises.solution_sql:
WITH marked AS (
        SELECT start_date, end_date,
               CASE WHEN LAG(end_date) OVER (ORDER BY start_date) = start_date
                    THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_project
        FROM project_days
      ), grouped AS (
        SELECT start_date, end_date,
               SUM(new_project) OVER (ORDER BY start_date) AS project_group
        FROM marked
      )
      SELECT MIN(start_date) AS project_start, MAX(end_date) AS project_end
      FROM grouped
      GROUP BY project_group
      ORDER BY project_end - project_start, project_start;
hints: Compare each start date with the previous row’s end date.
Mark a new group whenever the dates do not connect.
Use a running sum of the group marker, then aggregate each group.

exercises.title: Calculate a Three-Day Revenue Average

source.challenge: Calculate a rolling average of total revenue
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Calculate a rolling metric over the current row and a fixed number of preceding rows.

gate.course: PostgreSQL Summary Stats and Window Functions

exercises.scenario: Finance wants daily revenue shown beside a short moving average that smooths normal day-to-day changes.
exercises.task: Calculate the three-day rolling average revenue for every date.
result_requirements: Round the average to two decimals.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT revenue_date, revenue,
             ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (
               ORDER BY revenue_date
               ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
             ), 2) AS three_day_average
      FROM daily_revenue
      ORDER BY revenue_date;
hints: Order the window by revenue date.
A three-row window includes the current row and two preceding rows.
Place the frame clause inside the `OVER` parentheses.

exercises.title: Pivot Specialists into Role Columns

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Reshape category rows into aligned columns without losing names.

gate.course: PostgreSQL Summary Stats and Window Functions

exercises.scenario: A staffing brief needs one compact roster with a separate column for each specialty.
exercises.task: Pivot specialist names into `analyst`, `designer`, `engineer`, and `manager` columns.
result_requirements: Alphabetize names within each specialty before assigning row numbers.
Return the four specialty columns in the listed order.
Sort by the generated row number.
exercises.solution_sql:
WITH numbered AS (
        SELECT specialist_name, specialty,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                 PARTITION BY specialty
                 ORDER BY specialist_name
               ) AS row_num
        FROM specialists
      )
      SELECT
        MAX(CASE WHEN specialty = 'Analyst' THEN specialist_name END) AS analyst,
        MAX(CASE WHEN specialty = 'Designer' THEN specialist_name END) AS designer,
        MAX(CASE WHEN specialty = 'Engineer' THEN specialist_name END) AS engineer,
        MAX(CASE WHEN specialty = 'Manager' THEN specialist_name END) AS manager
      FROM numbered
      GROUP BY row_num
      ORDER BY row_num;
hints: Number names separately inside each specialty.
Use one conditional expression for each output column.
Group by the generated row number so names with the same position align.

exercises.title: Find Metric Values That Cannot Become Numbers

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Use safe conversion to identify values that do not match the intended numeric type.

gate.course: Functions for Manipulating Data in PostgreSQL

exercises.scenario: A metric import stores every value as text, and the data engineer needs the unusable rows identified before loading.
exercises.task: Return raw metric values that cannot be converted to a decimal number.
result_requirements: Do not treat valid zero or negative numbers as conversion failures.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT metric_id, metric_value
      FROM raw_metrics
      WHERE TRY_CAST(TRIM(metric_value) AS DECIMAL(12,2)) IS NULL
      ORDER BY metric_id;
hints: Use a conversion function that returns `NULL` instead of stopping on bad input.
Trim the text before converting it.
Filter the rows where the safe conversion result is null.

exercises.title: Calculate Booking End Times

source.challenge: Work out the end time of bookings
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Add a duration to a timestamp to calculate an end time.

gate.course: Functions for Manipulating Data in PostgreSQL

exercises.scenario: Facility bookings use 30-minute slots, and the scheduling screen needs each end time.
exercises.task: Calculate the end timestamp for every booking.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT booking_id, start_time,
             start_time + slots * INTERVAL '30 minutes' AS end_time
      FROM bookings
      ORDER BY start_time, booking_id;
hints: The duration equals the number of slots multiplied by 30 minutes.
DuckDB can add an interval directly to a timestamp.
Build the interval expression from `slots`, then alias the result `end_time`.

exercises.title: Separate New and Existing Monthly Users

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Compare each activity month with a user’s first activity month.

gate.course: Functions for Manipulating Data in PostgreSQL

exercises.scenario: Product analytics wants to see how many active users each month are new versus returning.
exercises.task: Count new and existing active users for each activity month.
result_requirements: A user is new when the activity month equals the user’s first activity month.
exercises.solution_sql:
WITH first_activity AS (
        SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_time)) AS first_month
        FROM user_events
        GROUP BY user_id
      ), monthly_activity AS (
        SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', event_time) AS activity_month
        FROM user_events
      )
      SELECT m.activity_month,
             COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.activity_month = f.first_month) AS new_users,
             COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.activity_month > f.first_month) AS existing_users
      FROM monthly_activity AS m
      INNER JOIN first_activity AS f ON m.user_id = f.user_id
      GROUP BY m.activity_month
      ORDER BY m.activity_month;
hints: First find each user’s earliest event month.
Create one row per user per activity month before counting.
Compare activity month with first month inside conditional counts.

exercises.title: Standardize Customer Phone Numbers

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Remove formatting characters from text while preserving the underlying digits.

gate.course: Functions for Manipulating Data in PostgreSQL

exercises.scenario: The CRM import needs phone values reduced to digits so matching rules work consistently.
exercises.task: Return every recorded phone number as digits only.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT customer_id,
             REGEXP_REPLACE(phone, '[^0-9]', '', 'g') AS phone_digits
      FROM customers
      WHERE phone IS NOT NULL
      ORDER BY customer_id;
hints: Keep only rows that have a phone value.
Use a regular expression that matches any non-digit character.
Replace every matching character with an empty string.

exercises.title: Format Customer Names for an Export

source.challenge: Format last names in uppercase and first names in lowercase
source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Apply text casing rules and build a formatted export value.

gate.course: Functions for Manipulating Data in PostgreSQL

exercises.scenario: A legacy partner requires names in a specific `LAST, first` format.
exercises.task: Format every customer name with the last name uppercase and the first name lowercase.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT customer_id,
             UPPER(last_name) || ', ' || LOWER(first_name) AS export_name
      FROM customers
      ORDER BY customer_id;
hints: Apply the casing functions before combining the values.
Include a comma and one space between the names.
Alias the final expression as `export_name`.

exercises.title: Search Support Subjects Without Case Sensitivity

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Find text regardless of capitalization.

gate.course: Functions for Manipulating Data in PostgreSQL

exercises.scenario: Quality assurance is reviewing any support case whose subject mentions a charge.
exercises.task: Return support cases whose subject contains the word `charge`, regardless of letter case.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT case_id, subject
      FROM support_cases
      WHERE subject ILIKE '%charge%'
      ORDER BY case_id;
hints: Use a pattern with wildcard characters on both sides of the search word.
The comparison should not depend on capitalization.
DuckDB supports `ILIKE` for case-insensitive matching.

exercises.title: Test Whether Email Is a Reliable Key

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Use duplicate and missing-value checks to evaluate a proposed business key.
exercises.scenario: A contact-import design proposes using email as the primary key, but the data architect wants evidence before approving it.
exercises.task: Summarize the problems that prevent `email` from being a reliable primary key.
result_requirements: `duplicate_email_rows` is the number of extra rows beyond the first occurrence of each non-null email.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT
        COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE email IS NULL) AS missing_emails,
        COUNT(email) - COUNT(DISTINCT email) AS duplicate_email_rows
      FROM raw_contacts;
hints: A primary key must be present on every row.
Compare the number of non-null email rows with the number of distinct emails.
The difference between those two counts is the number of extra duplicate rows.

exercises.title: Find Product Values That Break Normalization

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Identify repeated descriptive values that disagree for the same entity.
exercises.scenario: A denormalized order-line import repeats product details, and the data modeler needs to find products whose stored prices disagree.
exercises.task: Return products that have more than one distinct unit price in the raw order-line table.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT product_id,
             MIN(product_name) AS product_name,
             COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price) AS distinct_prices
      FROM raw_order_lines
      GROUP BY product_id
      HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price) > 1
      ORDER BY product_id;
hints: Group all repeated rows for the same product.
Count distinct prices inside each product group.
Use `HAVING` to keep only groups with more than one price.

exercises.title: Audit Broken Account Relationships

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Use an anti-join to find child rows that do not resolve to a valid parent.
exercises.scenario: Before a foreign-key rule is enforced, the database administrator needs a list of orders that would violate it.
exercises.task: Return orders whose account ID is missing or does not match an account.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.account_id, o.order_total
      FROM account_orders AS o
      LEFT JOIN accounts AS a ON o.account_id = a.account_id
      WHERE o.account_id IS NULL OR a.account_id IS NULL
      ORDER BY o.order_id;
hints: Preserve every order while attempting to match an account.
An unmatched non-null account leaves the joined account fields null.
Also include orders where the source account ID itself is null.

exercises.title: Assess VFX Delivery Performance

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.concept: Integrated joins, conditional aggregation, and percentages
exercises.learning_objective: Combine project and shot data into a decision-ready delivery summary.
exercises.scenario: A VFX production executive wants to know which projects are struggling to deliver completed shots on time.
exercises.task: Summarize final-shot delivery performance for each project.
result_requirements: Count a final shot as late when `delivery_date` is after `deadline`.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT p.project_name,
             COUNT(*) AS final_shots,
             COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.delivery_date > s.deadline) AS late_shots,
             ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.delivery_date <= s.deadline) / COUNT(*), 2) AS on_time_percentage
      FROM vfx_projects AS p
      INNER JOIN vfx_shots AS s ON p.project_id = s.project_id
      WHERE s.status = 'Final'
      GROUP BY p.project_name
      ORDER BY on_time_percentage, p.project_name;
hints: Filter to final shots before calculating project metrics.
Use conditional counts for late and on-time shots.
Multiply by `100.0` before division so the result is a percentage.

exercises.title: Find the Lowest-Revenue Restaurants

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Calculate revenue by entity and select the bottom-performing group.
exercises.scenario: A delivery marketplace is selecting two restaurants for a revenue-support pilot.
exercises.task: Return the two restaurants with the lowest total platform revenue.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT restaurant_name,
             ROUND(SUM(subtotal + service_fee), 2) AS total_revenue
      FROM restaurant_orders
      GROUP BY restaurant_name
      ORDER BY total_revenue, restaurant_name
      LIMIT 2;
hints: Calculate revenue for each order before summing.
Group to one row per restaurant.
Sort smallest to largest and keep the first two rows.

exercises.title: Calculate Workforce Cost by Team

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Join workforce tables and calculate regular and overtime labor cost.
exercises.scenario: Finance needs a team-level labor-cost summary that applies time-and-a-half to overtime hours.
exercises.task: Calculate total labor cost for each team.
result_requirements: Round hours and cost to two decimals.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT t.team_name,
             COUNT(DISTINCT w.worker_id) AS worker_count,
             ROUND(SUM(s.regular_hours + s.overtime_hours), 2) AS total_hours,
             ROUND(SUM(s.regular_hours * w.hourly_rate
                     + s.overtime_hours * w.hourly_rate * 1.5), 2) AS total_labor_cost
      FROM teams AS t
      INNER JOIN workers AS w ON t.team_id = w.team_id
      INNER JOIN shifts AS s ON w.worker_id = s.worker_id
      GROUP BY t.team_name
      ORDER BY total_labor_cost DESC, t.team_name;
hints: Start from teams and connect workers, then shifts.
Count workers distinctly because each worker can have several shifts.
Calculate regular and overtime cost inside the `SUM`.

exercises.title: Complete a Relational Data-Quality Audit

source.adaptation_note: Career Accelerator uses original wording, scenario, schema, records, expected output, hints, and solution.

exercises.learning_objective: Combine several integrity checks into one compact audit result.
exercises.scenario: A data engineer needs one audit table showing the number of key, relationship, and value problems in a raw customer-order extract.
exercises.task: Return issue counts for duplicate customer IDs, missing customer emails, orphaned orders, duplicate order IDs, and negative order amounts.
result_requirements: Use the exact issue labels `duplicate_customer_ids`, `missing_customer_emails`, `orphaned_orders`, `duplicate_order_ids`, and `negative_order_amounts`.
Include all five rows, even when a count is zero.
exercises.solution_sql:
SELECT 'duplicate_customer_ids' AS issue_type,
             COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS issue_count
      FROM audit_customers
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'missing_customer_emails', COUNT(*)
      FROM audit_customers
      WHERE email IS NULL
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'orphaned_orders', COUNT(*)
      FROM audit_orders AS o
      LEFT JOIN audit_customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL OR c.customer_id IS NULL
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'duplicate_order_ids', COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)
      FROM audit_orders
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'negative_order_amounts', COUNT(*)
      FROM audit_orders
      WHERE amount < 0
      ORDER BY issue_type;
hints: Write each audit check as a two-column query with a fixed issue label.
Use `UNION ALL` so every audit row is preserved.
Use a left anti-join pattern for orphaned orders, then sort the combined result.
